title: Synovial sarcoma reprograms transcription by GBAF activation of polycomb targets and loss of CBAF enhancers.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Synovial sarcoma reprograms transcription by GBAF activation of polycomb targets and loss of CBAF enhancers. Synovial sarcoma is a cancer driven by a fusion oncoprotein, SS18::SSX, that links SS18, a subunit of BAF-family chromatin remodeling complexes, to the carboxy terminus of SSX, which avidly binds nucleosomes with the histone post-translational modification H2AK119ub. Here, we show in mice that SS18::SSX expression redistributes non-canonical GBAF complexes broadly to promoters and distal enhancers marked by H2AK119ub, which causes developmental loci to lose H3K27me3 and become transcriptionally active. Canonical BAF containing SS18::SSX abandons its typical binding sites, is largely absent from H2AK119ub-marked sites, and instead distributes narrowly to transcription start sites with PBAF. Disruption of Arid1a or Arid1b (both CBAF-specific) retains synovial sarcoma character, while Smarcb1 (PBAF- and CBAF-specific) or Pbrm1 (PBAF-specific) disruption does not, although all accelerate SS18::SSX-driven tumorigenesis in mice. Thus, the synovial sarcomagenesis mechanism involves SS18::SSX reprogramming transcription positively through GBAF redistribution to activate polycomb-targeted developmental genes, and negatively by loss of normal CBAF localization and function.

evidence_text: NKG2A inhibition promotes NK cell-CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell interactions to improve anticancer immunity in ovarian carcinoma. Natural killer (NK) cells contribute to tumor immunosurveillance, yet their heterogeneity across cancer types remains incompletely understood. Transcriptomic, spatial, and functional assays reveal that non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) is enriched in NK cells that mediate clinically relevant effector functions, whereas high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) contains dysfunctional NK cells that express co-inhibitory receptors including NKG2A. Analysis of HGSOC patient samples and syngeneic mouse models indicates a crosstalk between NK cells and CD8⁺ T cells critical for effective antitumor immunity. Depletion of either population leads to phenotypic impairment of the reciprocal one. Blocking NKG2A restores NK cell cytotoxicity and promotes CD8⁺ T cell responses, significantly improving the efficacy of PD-1 blockade in murine HGSOC models. Thus, NK cells and CD8⁺ T cells engage in a functional interplay of immunological relevance. Moreover, the NKG2A-HLA-E axis represents a clinically actionable immunological checkpoint in tumors with impaired NK cell functions.

evidence_text: Comprehensive molecular characterization of craniopharyngiomas using whole transcriptome and spatial transcriptomics approaches. Craniopharyngiomas (CPs) are rare benign brain tumors that are classified as WHO grade I, with two subtypes: adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma (ACP) and papillary craniopharyngioma (PCP). ACP is caused by somatic mutations in exon 3 of the CTNNB1 gene activating the Wnt signaling pathway. PCP is associated with somatic BRAF p.V600E mutations activating the MAPK signaling pathway. Understanding their molecular differences is crucial for diagnosis and treatment. This study aimed to analyze common somatic alterations in ACP and PCP using bulk transcriptome sequencing and in situ spatial transcriptomics. RNA sequencing and high-resolution spatial profiling were used to detect mutations and examine gene expression differences among ACP, PCP, and healthy pituitary tissue. Whole transcriptome sequencing was performed on 24 tumor samples, with healthy pituitary data from the GTEx portal. Bioinformatics analysis utilized the CTAT mutation pipeline, with Sanger sequencing for validation. Results confirmed BRAF p.V600E mutations in all PCP samples and CTNNB1 mutations in all ACP samples. Differential gene expression analysis highlighted distinct molecular profiles and reinforced the involvement of Wnt and MAPK signaling. Spatial profiling identified 41 differentially expressed genes between ACP and PCP. This study provides critical insights into CP biology, supporting improved diagnostics and potential therapeutic strategies.

evidence_text:
High Treg and PMN-MDSC densities are a hallmark of tertiary lymphoid structures in fatal cases of cervical cancer.

Background

High densities of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) are associated with improved clinical outcomes in various malignancies, including human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). However, the role of TLSs in shaping antitumor immunity in HPV-induced cervical cancer (CESC) remains unclear. Therefore, we analyzed the density, composition, and prognostic impact of TLSs in patients with CESC as well as patients with HNSCC.

Methods

Multiplex immunofluorescence, immunohistochemistry, and spatial transcriptomics were used to analyze TLS density and composition in HNSCC and CESC tissue sections with respect to patient prognosis. The spatial approach was supplemented by flow cytometry-based analysis of the polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cell (PMN-MDSC) phenotype in freshly resected primary tumor tissues.

Results

Although both indications were associated with HPV infection, we confirmed a positive correlation between TLS density and improved overall survival only in patients with HNSCC. The TLS composition differed markedly between HNSCC and CESC samples, with a shift toward high regulatory T cell (Treg) and PMN-MDSC abundance in CESC samples. The highest Treg and PMN-MDSC levels were observed in patients with CESC who died of the disease. CESC-infiltrating PMN-MDSCs showed high arginase 1 expression, which correlated with diminished T-cell receptor (TCR)ζ chain expression in CESC-infiltrating T cells. Additionally, the high number of PMN-MDSCs in TLSs was associated with the absence of HPV-specific T cells in CESC.

Conclusions

Unlike in HNSCC, the composition of TLSs, rather than their quantity, was associated with the overall survival of patients with CESC. High numbers of Tregs and PMN-MDSCs infiltrating immature TLSs prevail in patients with CESC who succumbed to the disease and seem to affect tumor-specific immune responses.

evidence_text: Reconstructing 3D transcriptional organization from spatial transcriptomics reveals consistent oncogenic translocations and developmental dynamics. Reconstructing the 3D spatial organization of transcription from 2D spatial data is a fundamental challenge in genomics. Here, we introduce Cytocraft, a computational framework that addresses this problem by inferring a shared, cell-type-specific 3D configuration of transcription centers from subcellular spatial transcriptomics profiles. After validating Cytocraft's robust accuracy in simulations (median relative error: 0.0346), we applied it to diverse datasets to explore spatial patterns that may reflect underlying transcriptional organization. In human nonsmall cell lung cancer, we observed consistent spatial repositioning patterns, suggesting that the marker MALAT1 may undergo directional translocation during malignant transformation across eight patient samples. In the developing axolotl brain, we found that transcription center reorganization exhibits conserved developmental dynamics across distinct cell types, suggesting coordinated developmental dynamics. By enabling 3D reconstruction of transcription center configurations from 2D data, Cytocraft provides a powerful tool to explore the spatial organization of transcription in development and disease.

evidence_text: Deciphering precursor cell dynamics in esophageal preneoplasia via genetic barcoding and single-cell transcriptomics. Although histologically normal, esophageal preneoplastic cells harbor early genetic alterations and likely exhibit lineage plasticity. However, their origins and trajectories remain unclear. To address this, we combined genetic barcoding with single-cell RNA sequencing to trace the lineage of esophageal preneoplastic cells. We identified a distinct progenitor-like cell population with high plasticity. Through a scoring system, these high-plasticity cells are mapped, revealing their contributions to proliferative and basal cell populations. This approach uncovers molecular markers, including Nfib and Qk, that define these precursor cells, validated by spatial transcriptomics and a Trp53 Cdkn2a Notch1 mouse model. These findings provide critical insights into early tumorigenesis, highlighting the potential of precursor cells as biomarkers for early detection and therapeutic targets of esophageal squamous cell cancer. By elucidating the cellular dynamics underlying esophageal preneoplasia, this research lays the foundation for strategies to prevent malignant progression, offering broader implications for improving cancer diagnostics and treatment approaches.

evidence_text: A tissue multiplexing approach to maximize spatial omics output from pathology specimens. Spatial profiling technologies are revolutionising traditional research by enabling whole transcriptome and high-plex protein in situ analysis at scale. Profiling tissue microarrays permits multiple specimens to be analysed at once, but depending upon your research question, these are not widely applicable. Since diagnostic specimens retrieved from pathology laboratories cannot be altered (aside from sectioning) for ethico-legal reasons, this method introduces an approach in which multiple patient specimens, sectioned from individual tissue blocks, are combined to enable measurement of several tissues within a single capture array. This strategy provides a cost-effective means to increase sample size, permitting statistically robust data outputs, and fast-tracks clinical implementation. Importantly, our tissue multiplexing method is compatible with the standard protocols of multiple spatial platforms, including Visium CytAssist (and HD), Xenium in situ, GeoMx, CosMx, PhenoCycler-Fusion, and MERSCOPE. We have used skin biopsies in this study as this is our primary area of research, but this method can be extended to any tissue of interest.

evidence_text:
Application of CTC-derived spheroid for drug screening toward personalized treatment in patients with breast cancer.

Purpose

Tumor heterogeneity and drug resistance remain key challenges in breast cancer management. While organoid cultures can be established from resected tumor specimens, patients undergoing systematic treatment often lack accessible tissue for ex vivo drug testing. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) offer a minimally invasive alternative. The purpose of this study was to establish a clinically feasible workflow that integrates CTC enumeration and CTC-derived spheroid drug screening to overcome the limitations of tissue-dependent organoid models and enable personalized treatment in breast cancer.

Methods

CTCs were isolated from 34 newly diagnosed breast cancer patients using a liposome-tethered supported lipid bilayer (LIPO-SLB) microfluidic platform functionalized with anti-EpCAM antibodies. Thirteen patients undergoing systemic therapy and relapse were further assessed using CTC-spheroid culture for ex vivo drug screening. Hormone receptor expression and genomic mutation profiles were integrated with drug testing. One relapsed case underwent pre- and post-treatment spatial transcriptomic analysis (Xenium in situ).

Results

CTC and CTC-cluster counts significantly declined post-treatment in responders (p=0.044 and p=0.0264, respectively), but not in non-responders. CTC-spheroids were successfully generated in all 13 cases, enabling ex vivo drug testing. Effective therapies were identified in 9 patients (69.2%), of whom 7 achieved partial responses and 1 achieved stable disease; one patient did not receive the suggested treatment. Ex vivo drug sensitivity results correlated with clinical outcomes. Integrating CTC-based drug testing, hormone receptor expression in CTCs, and genomic DNA mutation profile further improved prediction of radiological response. Spatial transcriptomics revealed therapy-induced clonal shifts, with resistant subpopulations characterized by over-expression of chemoresistant gene, EIF4EBP1.

Conclusion

This study demonstrates that CTC-derived spheroid drug screening provides actionable therapeutic guidance when tissue is unavailable. Combined with hormone receptor and genomic profiling, this liquid biopsy-based platform enables personalized treatment, and dynamic monitoring of resistance in breast cancer.

evidence_text: Spatial single-cell multi-omics characterization of the tumor microenvironment heterogeneity by HER-2 expression status in gastric cancer. BACKGROUND: The success of novel antibody-drug conjugates, such as trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) and disitamab vedotin (RC48), has been pivotal in rendering “HER-2-low” gastric cancer (GC) a therapeutically targetable entity, expanding the population benefiting from anti-HER2 therapy by 2-3-fold. This advancement underscores the imperative to redefine and subclassify HER-2 status in GC. In this study, we innovatively proposed a four-tiered HER-2 classification standard for GC and, for the first time, conducted comparative analyses at the spatial single-cell multi-omics level across these four subgroups. METHODS: HER-2 status was recategorized into absent (immunohistochemistry (IHC) 0+, HER2_N), low (IHC 1+, HER2_L), moderate (IHC 2+/fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)-, HER2_M), and high (IHC 2+/FISH + or IHC 3+, HER2_H) groups. Primary tumor samples from 427 GC patients were collected and analyzed using Xenium5K in situ single-cell spatial transcriptomics (n = 153) and multiplex immunofluorescence (n = 427) detection base on tissue microassays. RESULTS: The proportion of samples that classified as HER2_N, HER2_L, HER2_M, and HER2_H was 43.13%, 22.88%, 11.11%, and 22.88%, respectively. Spatial HER-2 heterogeneous expression existed in 74.42% of HER-2 expressing GC and in 40.0% of HER2_H cases, which correlated with an unfavorable response to combined HER-2-targeted and immunotherapy and poor prognosis. In HER2_H group, lower infiltrates of exhausted T cells and regulatory T cells (Treg), higher cytotoxic activity of T cells, and enriched T cell-B cell niches were discovered, presenting a favorable tumor microenvironment that may benefit from immunotherapy. In HER2_M population, significantly higher CTLA4 + Treg infiltration, and their strengthened interactions with other cells via the CD80/CD86-CTLA4 axis were highlighted. HER2_L group exhibited increased infiltrates of SOX2-OT + mesenchymal cells and TGF-β-driven stromal-tumor cellular interactions. Moreover, HER2_N group presented a higher prevalence of diffuse and mixed histology, enriched endothelial cell-fibroblast-myeloid-derived suppressor cell niches, and augmented angiogenic activity. CONCLUSION: Differences in clinicopathologic, molecular, and immunological underpinnings were underscored across GC with differential HER-2 expression status, providing a rationale for a novel quaternary HER-2 classification system and the development of stratified therapeutic strategies.

evidence_text: Induced B cell receptor diversity predicts PD-1 blockade immunotherapy response. Immune checkpoint inhibitors such as anti-Programmed Death-1 antibodies (aPD-1) can be effective in treating advanced cancers. However, many patients do not respond, and the mechanisms underlying these differences remain incompletely understood. In this study, we profile a cohort of patients with locally advanced or metastatic basal cell carcinoma undergoing aPD-1 therapy using single-cell RNA sequencing, high-definition spatial transcriptomics in tumors and draining lymph nodes, and spatial immunoreceptor profiling, with long-term clinical follow-up. We find that successful responses to PD-1 inhibition are characterized by an induction of B cell receptor (BCR) clonal diversity after treatment initiation. These induced BCR clones spatially colocalize with T cell clones, facilitate their activation, and traffic alongside them between tumor and draining lymph nodes to enhance tumor clearance. Furthermore, we validated aPD-1-induced BCR diversity as a predictor of clinical response in a larger cohort of glioblastoma, melanoma, and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma patients, suggesting that this is a generalizable predictor of treatment response across many types of cancers. We find that pretreatment tumors harbor a characteristic gene expression signature that portends a higher probability of inducing BCR clonal diversity after aPD-1 therapy, and we develop a machine learning model that predicts PD-1-induced BCR clonal diversity from baseline tumor RNA sequencing. These findings underscore a dynamic role of B cell diversity during immunotherapy, highlighting its importance as a prognostic marker and a potential target for intervention in non-responders.

evidence_text:
Single-cell spatial analysis identifies ID1-high endothelial cells in tertiary lymphoid structures as predictors of durable response to immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer. BACKGROUND: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) maturity and cellular composition shape resistance or sensitivity to immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) across cancers. Single-cell spatial resolution data for the endothelial compartment of TLSs are lacking; therefore, we investigated the cellular composition, endothelial dynamics, and cell-cell interactions within TLS regions. METHODS: We applied high-resolution Xenium In Situ spatial transcriptomics to eight samples collected from non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLC) (four after chemoimmunotherapy, four untreated), extracted 90 TLS regions, generated approximately 320,000 single-cell profiles from those regions, and analyzed the endothelial compartment within each TLS. We independently assessed the exploratory findings using multiplex immunofluorescence and survival analysis in a separate cohort of 45 patients receiving immunotherapy. RESULTS: Spatial mapping revealed a reproducible, B-cell-dominant TLS architecture across all samples. Mature TLSs contained CXCL13-rich follicular cores and were associated with a favorable prognosis. Within the endothelial compartment, high endothelial cells (HECs) forming high-endothelial venules (HEVs) segregated from other endothelial cells; in mature TLSs these HECs exhibited high inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1) expression and an adhesion molecular signature, promoting lymphocyte recruitment. Patients with tumors harboring ID1-high HEVs showed higher response rates and pronounced survival advantage; multivariable analysis confirmed ID1-high status as an independent prognostic factor. Conversely, ICB exposure eventually reduced ID1 expression and adhesion molecule levels in HECs, impaired lymphocyte trafficking, and promoted a shift toward a remodeled endothelial state. CONCLUSIONS: ID1expression, linked to HEC differentiation during TLS maturation or ICB exposure, marks a functionally mature, lymphocyte-recruiting HEV that predict durable response to immunotherapy. These findings provide a novel mechanistic framework and practical biomarkers for HEV-centered immuno-oncology strategies in NSCLC. Introduction  Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide [ 1 ]. Platinum-based chemoimmunotherapy combining cytotoxic agents with immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) has extended survival in some patients and is standard both as a neoadjuvant setting and a first-line treatment for advanced disease [ 2 – 5 ]. Despite ongoing real-world data analyses, reliable biomarkers capable of definitively distinguishing durable responders from non-responders are needed [ 6 ,  7 ].  The presence and maturity of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) within the tumor microenvironment have emerged as key prognostic and predictive elements across multiple solid tumors [ 8 – 10 ]. In NSCLC, the densities of DC-LAMP⁺ mature dendritic cells and CD20⁺ B cells within TLSs are correlated with long-term survival [ 11 ,  12 ]. Mature TLSs are linked to favorable ICI response in various types of cancers, such as NSCLC and bladder cancer, and then high levels of intra-tumoral CXCL13 expression mark patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer likely to respond to treatment [ 13 ,  14 ].  The canonical 12-chemokine “TLS gene signature” is employed to predict TLS regions in transcriptomic analyses [ 15 ,  16 ]. However, its expression varies across tumor types, underscoring the inter-cancer TLS heterogeneity and the need for more tumor-specific functional TLS markers [ 17 ]. Our re-analysis of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data to isolate TLS-like cells with the 12-chemokine scores yielded few B-cell populations in breast ( n  = 26) and lung ( n  = 185) cancer samples (Supplementary Fig. S1A, B) [ 18 ,  19 ], highlighting the limitations of dissociative single-cell methods for analyzing structured niches. Therefore, spatially resolved transcriptomics is essential for capturing TLS architecture and heterogeneity in situ.  Previous studies have investigated spatial transcriptomics focused on TLS [ 20 – 22 ]. Immature TLSs enriched with immunosuppressive macrophages and regulatory T cells confer resistance to ICB, particularly in peritoneal metastases in gastric cancer [ 23 ]. Additionally, tumors containing mature TLSs can exhibit primary ICB resistance driven by distinct cancer-associated fibroblast subsets (FAP⁺ αSMA⁺ and MYH11⁺ αSMA⁺) in NSCLC [ 24 ]. Collectively, these studies demonstrated the effects of both TLS maturity and cellular composition on therapeutic outcomes. However, to date, the spatiotemporal dynamics of endothelial cells within TLSs have not been assessed using single-cell resolution methods.  Therefore, the present study applied high-resolution Xenium In Situ spatial single-cell transcriptomics to resected NSCLC specimens. We investigated the cellular components, endothelial cell dynamics, and cell–cell interactions within TLS associated region by TLS maturity and treatment status with or without chemo-immunotherapy. The study design is shown in Fig.  1 . The resulting dataset provides a foundational atlas of TLS regions in NSCLC and highlights inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1)-high endothelial venules (HEVs) as a potential biomarker, offering insights to guide new immunotherapeutic approaches or enhance the effectiveness of current treatments.    Fig. 1   Study design and cohorts. ( A ) Xenium discovery cohort: profiling of eight resected NSCLC specimens (four neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, four untreated) using spatial single-cell transcriptomics allowed the manual annotation of 90 TLS regions for downstream analyses. ( B ) Biomarker validation cohort: 45 archival NSCLC resections from patients treated with immune-checkpoint blockade after recurrence were interrogated by multiplex immunofluorescence for TLS/HEV markers and linked to overall patient survival                     Materials and methods   Patients and samples  Tissue specimens and clinical records from patients with NSCLC were collected at 14 Japanese institutions between January 2017 and February 2024. Consistent with the KEYNOTE-189, CheckMate-816, and CheckMate-9LA protocols [ 2 ,  4 ,  5 ], patients harboring major EGFR mutations or ALK rearrangements were excluded.  In the xenium discovery cohort, we initially identified 29 patients who underwent surgical resection within the preceding two years, with or without neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy. Patients who achieved clinical complete response after the neoadjuvant therapy or received perioperative radiotherapy were excluded. Furthermore, we selected eight patients showing TLSs enrichment in immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis (as described below) and with an RNA DV200 ≥ 30%. Given the limited tissue from pre-treatment bronchoscopic biopsies, matched pre-/post-treatment pairs were not available, and independent resected specimens were used for Xenium analysis. Therefore, the final analysis included four patients who received neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy and four patients who underwent surgery without neoadjuvant chemotherapy, analyzed as independent patient samples (Supplementary Fig. S2A, B). In the biomarker validation cohort using multiplex-immunofluorescence (MIF), 683 patients who underwent ICB with or without chemotherapy were initially screened. Among these, 575 patients were excluded because the available specimens were derived from bronchoscopy, metastatic-site biopsy, computed tomography-guided needle biopsy, or because no residual tissue remained. Archived lung specimens obtained prior to any immunotherapy exposure were available from 108 surgical cases. Among these, 45 patients who later initiated immunotherapy within two years after postoperative recurrence were enrolled for MIF (as described below), and survival analysis (Supplementary Fig. S3).  Additionally, we retrieved a scRNA-seq dataset comprising 26 breast cancer specimens from the GEO (accession  GSE176078 ) and downloaded an integrated scRNA-seq dataset of 185 NSCLC specimens from Figshare (DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.6222221.v3).    Treatment responses and survival evaluation  Clinical variables, including age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, smoking history, histology, programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score (PD-L1 TPS), clinical stage, and treatment outcomes, were extracted from patient records. PD-L1 TPS was measured with the 22C3 antibody. Radiographic responses were categorized according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1 [ 25 ]. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from chemo-immunotherapy initiation to death or the last follow-up. The data cut-off date was March 31, 2025.    IHC and MIF examination  Chromogenic IHC was performed on 5 μm formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) lung-cancer sections after Tris-EDTA retrieval (pH 9.0, 95 °C, 40 min) and peroxidase quenching (Dako REAL). Serial sections were incubated at 4 °C overnight with primary antibodies including anti-CD3 (Proteintech, #60181-1-Ig, 1:800), anti-CD20 (Proteintech, #60271-1-Ig, 1:1000), and anti-PNAd (BioLegend, clone MECA-79, #120801, 1:100). Detection was performed using an HRP–DAB system following the manufacturers’ instructions. MIF was performed with two four-marker panels. Panel 1: CD20 (Abcam, #ab194970, 1:200), CD23-CL594 (Proteintech, clone 4C7C9, #CL594-60208-2, 1:100), CD3-CL647 (Proteintech, clone 3F3A1, #CL647-60181, 1:100), and CXCL12 (CST, clone D8G6H, #97958, 1:100); Panel 2: MECA-79-AF488 (Invitrogen, clone MECA-79, #53-6-36–82, 1:50), CD31 (Proteintech, clone 3F8E2, #66065-2-Ig, 1:100), CD20 (Abcam, #ab194970, 1:200), and ID1 (CST, clone F2M1J, #23369, 1:100).  Fluorescence was detected using the following secondary antibodies: donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 488, donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 647, donkey anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 594 (Invitrogen, 1:500, 1 h, room temperature), and goat anti-rabbit CoraLite Plus 750 (Proteintech, 1:200, 1 h, RT). The slides were mounted in antifade medium with DAPI (Invitrogen) and imaged on an FV3000 confocal microscope (Olympus) with 20×, 40×, and 60× objectives under identical laser and gain settings.    IHC quantification  TLSs were identified with a two-step procedure as previously described [ 26 ]. First, serial sections were immunostained for CD20 (B cells), CD3 (T cells), and PNAd (HEV). TLS-positive specimens showed clusters of T cells surrounding aggregates of B cells. Second, TLSs were divided into three status by B-cell density and follicular architecture: absent, immature, and mature. CXCL12 protein level was quantified using ImageJ (v 2.9.0/1.53t) as the mean percentage of the TLS area with positive staining in three representative fields. Cases above and below the cohort median (excluding TLS-negative samples) were classified as CXCL12-high and CXCL12-low, respectively. ID1 status was determined by counting ID1-positive endothelial cells in HEVs within TLSs across three representative microscopic fields. Specimens with a mean count ≥ 10 and < 10 cells were classified as ID1-high and ID1-low, respectively. Two investigators trained in digital histopathology reviewed the images independently and were blinded to the clinical data. Discrepancies were resolved by joint review, and the final status was verified by an additional pathologist.    Xenium in situ workflow  Five-micron FFPE sections (DV200 ≥ 30%) containing TLSs by IHC were processed using the Xenium FFPE workflow (see 10x Genomics,  CG000601  Rev B). After de-paraffinization, decrosslinking, and Tris-EDTA retrieval, the slides were hybridized overnight at 50 °C with a 430-gene probe set (10 nM each, 380-gene Human Immune-Oncology base panel plus 50 custom endothelial-focused custom genes; Supplementary Table S1), then ligated and amplified by rolling-circle amplification. The prepared slides were run on the Xenium Analyzer, which executed 15 automated cycles of fluorescent probe binding, imaging, and stripping, capturing 0.75 μm Z-stacks across the entire 12 × 24 mm imaging area. The on-instrument pipeline stitched fields of view, segmented nuclei/cells from DAPI, and decoded transcripts by maximum-likelihood matching to the gene codebook. Transcripts with calibrated Q-scores ≥ 20 were retained. A cell-by-gene count matrix, segmentation masks; and morphology images were exported for downstream analysis.    Xenium in situ analyses  Cell segmentation morphology images generated by the Xenium Analyzer were co-registered with the corresponding H&E images, after which every TLS was manually delineated, and the constituent cells were extracted for downstream analysis (Supplementary Fig. S4). TLS boundaries were drawn to encompass contiguous clusters of immune cells. All spatial transcriptomic analyses in this study were restricted to cells located within these manually annotated TLS regions of interest. Tumor parenchyma outside the TLS boundaries was not included in the expression matrices used for any downstream analyses.  All analyses were carried out using R software (v 4.4.2) and Python (v 3.12.9). Using Seurat package (v 5.2.1), we generated a separate Seurat object for each TLS and removed low-quality cells (< 5 detected genes and < 10 total transcript counts). All TLS objects were then pooled into a single Seurat object for downstream processing. Gene expression matrices were normalized using the NormalizeData function, variable features were identified with the FindVariableFeatures function, and linear scaling was applied using the ScaleData function. PCA was performed with the RunPCA function and the optimal number of principal components (PCs) was selected from the ElbowPlot. Batch effects arising from sample identity were corrected by applying the RunHarmony function to the PCA embeddings, and clustering was conducted on the Harmony-integrated PCs using the Louvain algorithm [ 27 ]. The same embeddings were used to generate Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualizations.  Because spatial transcriptomics can misassign transcripts to neighboring cells, the cell-type annotation did not rely solely on canonical markers. Rather, candidate markers for each cluster were identified using FindMarkers function (log fold-change > 0.20;  P  < 0.01), and the resulting labels were imported into Xenium Explorer, where they were cross-validated against cellular morphology and histological context (e.g., endothelial cells continuity). Higher-resolution analyses were performed for endothelial cells, with each population re-extracted into a new Seurat object, dimensional reduction and clustering repeated as described above, and cell-type identities refined (Supplementary Table S2) [ 15 ,  28 – 31 ]. Mixed clusters were similarly reclassified, and the final cell-type labels were appended to the metadata of the main object.  Differentially expressed genes were identified for each cell type with two-sided t-tests, with significance thresholds of |log₂ fold change| ≥ 0.20 and  P  < 0.01. Genes that met these criteria were subjected to Gene Ontology overrepresentation analysis to elucidate the biological pathways that were preferentially affected in each comparison. Cell–cell communications (CCIs) were reconstructed using CellChat package (v 2.1.2), which quantitatively infers ligand–receptor interaction networks from scRNA-seq profiles. To place these interactions in their spatial context, we subsequently analyzed the CCIs within each field of view, including TLSs, using stLearn (v 0.4.10).    Statistical analyses  Continuous variables and dichotomous variables are summarized as medians with inter-quartile ranges and absolute counts with percentages, respectively. Group differences in categorical data were assessed with Pearson’s χ² or Fisher’s exact tests, as appropriate. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare TLS counts and the cellular compositions stratified by TLS maturity and treatment arm. OS was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier curves (log-rank test) and modelled using Cox proportional-hazards regression. The independent correlates of TLS maturation and CXCL12/ID1 status were identified with multivariable logistic regression. All analyses were performed in R (v 4.4.2), and two-sided P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.     Results   Spatial single-cell atlas reveals B-cell-dominated TLS architecture independent of neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy  The eight-patient Xenium discovery cohort is summarized in Table  1 . Apart from a slightly younger median age in the ICB plus chemotherapy arm, the two groups were well balanced for sex, clinical stage, histological subtype and PD-L1 TPS. Neoadjuvant treatment produced one pathological complete response, with partial responses in the remaining cases. A density map from Xenium Explorer demonstrated that a composite oncogenic signature, based on  CEACAM6 ,  EGFR ,  EPCAM ,  ERBB2 ,  ERBB3 ,  MET ,  MUC5AC  and  TMPRSS2 , closely tracked with therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, serial sections confirmed PNAd-positive HEV in all TLSs (Supplementary Fig. S5). After filtering, 319,909 cells were retained and classified based on canonical markers into 16 cell-type clusters: conventional B cells (Bconv), follicular B cells (FoB), proliferating B cells, conventional CD4⁺ T cells (CD4_Tconv), follicular-helper T cells (Tfh), regulatory T cells (Treg), CD8⁺ T cells, plasma cells, macrophages, mature and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (mDC, pDC), mast cells, neutrophils, endothelial cells, fibroblasts and tumor cells (Fig.  2 A). Unintegrated UMAPs showed specimen-specific clustering; however, harmony correction merged cells from all eight samples into shared lineage islands, indicating effective removal of batch effects (Fig.  2 B). CXCR5  peaked in FoB and Tfh cells, whereas  FCER2  was highest in FoB and proliferating B cells. The cellular composition was strikingly reproducible across patients. B-cell subsets dominated, with Bconv (18.5%) and FoB (17.6%) together comprising ~ 36%, and proliferating B cells adding 2.8%. T-cell populations accounted for ~ 33%: CD4_Tconv 17.7%, CD8⁺ T 11.4%, Tfh 2.2% and Treg 1.6%. Myeloid cells were less abundant (macrophages 4.5%, mDCs 1.0%), and each remaining cell-types, including endothelial and fibroblast cells, accounted for roughly 8% of the compartment (Fig.  2 E). Overall, spatial single-cell mapping yielded a reproducible B-cell-centered TLS atlas that was consistent across all samples.    TLS maturation reshapes immune niches and improves survival under cancer immunotherapy  To minimize therapy-related bias, TLS maturation was interrogated exclusively in untreated controls. Representative Xenium Explorer and MIF findings readily distinguished compact, mantle-ringed B-cell follicles from loosely organized, T-cell–rich aggregates, designating the former as mature and the latter as immature.  CXCL13 ,  CXCR5 ,  FCER2  and  MS4A1  were highly concentrated in mature cores; their combined expression was converted into a “mature-TLS score” with AddModuleScore function (Fig.  3 A) [ 34 ,  35 ]. Using a threshold of 0 separated 22 mature (≥ 0) and 26 immature (< 0) structures (Fig.  3 B), and visual overlays of TLS maturation showed near-perfect concordance with histology (Fig.  3 C). Area-normalized transcriptional profiling of the 13 chemokines and their receptors revealed a sharp dichotomy (Fig.  3 D): mature TLSs contained significantly more  CXCL13  and  CXCR4 , whereas immature TLSs were enriched for  CCL2 ,  CCL3 ,  CCL4 ,  CCL5 ,  CCL8 ,  CCL18  and the IFN-inducible  CXCL9–11  cluster. TLS-area–adjusted cell counts mirrored these findings, with higher densities of every B-cell subset in mature TLSs, and predominantly CD8⁺ T cells, macrophages, mDCs and endothelial cells in their immature counterparts (Fig.  3 E). In mature TLSs, fibroblasts showed higher  CXCL12 , whereas FoBs exhibited elevated  CXCR4  [ 36 ]. Tfh cells expressed abundant  CXCL13  together with  CXCR5  on B cells [ 33 ]. In contrast, immature TLSs exhibited a Th1-skewed inflammatory milieu characterized by  CXCL9  from IFN-γ-responsive macrophages and DCs, and higher  IFIT3  in CD8⁺ T cells. Endothelial transcriptomics reinforced this functional divergence: mature TLS vasculature preferentially expressed PNAd-associated genes, such as  CHST4  and  B3GNT3  together with adhesion molecules, including  SELP  and  ICAM1 , whereas immature TLSs overexpressed the HEV-developmental receptors  LTBR  and  TNFRSF14  (Fig.  3 F and Supplementary Fig. S6). Kaplan–Meier curves in immunotherapy-treated patients demonstrated that mature TLSs conferred a substantial survival advantage over immature or absent TLSs (median OS 60.2 vs. 21.4 months; log-rank  P  = 0.037) (Fig.  3 H). Collectively, these spatial and transcriptional features characterize TLS maturation states and demonstrate their prognostic relevance in patients receiving immunotherapy. The HEC cluster was characterized by robust expression of classical HEV genes, including  ACKR1 ,  SELP ,  LTBR  and  TNFRSF14 , confirming its HEV-like phenotype (Fig.  4 B) [ 30 ]. MIF of resected samples corroborated the spatial coexistence of both HEC- and BEC-type vessels within mature TLSs in situ (Fig.  4 C). Differential-expression analysis of HECs revealed significant upregulation of  ID1  in mature TLSs compared with immature TLSs (Fig.  4 D,  P  < 0.05). Compared with the other ID family members,  ID2  and  ID4 ,  ID1  was selectively expressed in endothelial cells, with the highest levels observed in HECs (Fig.  4 E, F). We further re-analyzed an integrated scRNA-seq dataset comprising 185 NSCLC samples to validate ID-family expression in the vascular compartment [ 19 ].  ID1  expression was largely confined to malignant epithelial and endothelial cells. Within the endothelial lineage, its expression was observed across several subpopulations, including mature HECs. In mature HECs,  ID1  was frequently expressed, whereas  ID2  and  ID4  were rarely detected (Supplementary Fig. S8). Furthermore, spatial CCI maps demonstrated that TLSs in ICB–treated tumors displayed stronger  CXCL12–CXCR4  signaling than those in untreated controls (Fig.  5 F). Within this pathway, fibroblasts showed the strongest communication probabilities with follicular B cells (Fig.  5 G). Nearest-neighbor distances between fibroblasts and FoBs were comparable in the control and ICB cohort (Fig.  5 H). ICB–treated tumors contained fewer PNAd-positive HEV per square millimeter than control, indicating a treatment-related reduction in HEV density (Fig.  6 A, B). TLS-associated HECs from ICB–treated tumors exhibited a transcriptional shift in which adhesion genes including  SELE  and  SELP  together with the PNAd-biosynthetic module — B3GNT3 ,  CHST4 ,  FUT7 ,  GCNT1  and  ST3GAL4 — were likewise suppressed, and the differentiation brake  ID1  fell sharply, along with  ID2  (Fig.  6 C, D). In contrast, angio-remodeling transcripts, including  ANGPT1 ,  ANGPT2 ,  VEGFA ,  APLN ,  APLNR , and  FLT1 , increased. However, VEGFA expression within endothelial cells was minimal, and the ligand was predominantly supplied by fibroblasts rather than by HEVs themselves (Supplementary Fig. 10). Gene Ontology analysis consistently shows that ICB therapy redirected HECs from an immune-recruitment program toward vascular remodeling: genes that are upregulated in the treated group clustered within angiogenesis pathways, whereas those enriched in controls were related to immune trafficking (Fig.  6 E). Furthermore, ICB therapy significantly decreased an adhesion signature per TLS, defined by  B3GNT3 ,  CHST4 ,  FUT7 ,  GCNT1 ,  ST3GAL4 ,  SELE ,  SELP ,  ICAM1  and  VCAM1 , while simultaneously amplifying an angio-remodel signature comprising  ANGPT1 ,  ANGPT2 ,  APLN ,  APLNR ,  FLT1  and  TEK  (Fig.  6 F, G). Functionally, the normalized counts of conventional B, CD4⁺ T, and CD8⁺ T cells located within 100 μm of a HEC were significantly reduced in the ICB cohort (Fig.  6 H,  P  < 0.05). Finally, MIF showed markedly reduced ID1 protein in TLS-associated HECs from ICB–treated tumors compared with controls, mirroring the transcriptomic downregulation described above (Fig.  6 I, J). In summary, TLS-associated HEVs potentially shift phenotypically with TLS maturation and treatment. In immature TLS, HEVs first express the LTβR axis and homing chemokines, recruiting lymphocytes via nascent HEC cuffs with BECs. During maturation,  ID1  increases, and classical adhesion features together with the PNAd-synthetic enzyme set predominates, yielding a fully functional “mature HEV.” ICB ultimately regresses tumors and drives the vessels into a remodeled endothelial state: ID1 levels fall sharply, the adhesion/PNAd module contracts, and lymphocyte influx diminishes, while vascular-remodeling genes are induced, preserving structural plasticity (Fig.  6 K). In the present study, we aimed to map how TLS composition and endothelial dynamics varied with maturation and treatment, and link these mechanistic insights to clinical outcomes to elucidate their contribution to TLS-mediated antitumor immunity.  This study provides an integrated spatial-omics framework unifying the cellular and clinical dimensions of TLSs in NSCLC, particularly in endothelial populations. By combining high-sensitivity in situ transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence, and immunotherapy-related clinical outcomes, we delineate three key principles: (i) TLS maturation establishes novel immune niches in NSCLC, (ii) ID1-high HEVs within mature TLSs confer clinical benefit, and (iii) ICB therapy reprograms HEVs from a lymphocyte-recruiting phenotype to a vascular-reprogramming state while enhancing a  CXCL12-CXCR4  niche.  Spatial transcriptomics is indispensable for analyzing TLS biology. TLSs juxtapose lymphoid, myeloid, and stromal elements in complex three-dimensional assemblies. Therefore, only methods that preserve tissue coordinates and resolve individual cells can reveal their true organization. The Xenium In Situ platforms provide sub-micrometer, in-situ detection of transcripts, enabling the visual validation of cell annotations and tracking of follicles, vessels, and related microstructure continuity throughout an entire TLS. By applying this platform, we profiled > 300,000 TLS-resident cells at single-cell resolution to obtain a nearly exhaustive annotation of every anatomical component. We further expanded the standard immuno-oncology panel with vascular-specific genes, allowing cytokine and chemokine quantification across all cell types, with a focus on endothelial cells.  Consistent with our observations, studies in both hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer show that mature TLSs are characterized by  CXCL13 -rich, B-cell-dominated cores, whereas immature aggregates show enrichment of  CXCL9-11  and Th1-skewed signatures [ 23 ,  39 ]. While single-cell studies on HEVs in human tumors are limited, analogous analyses in human lymph nodes are increasing [ 30 ,  40 ]. These nodal datasets have demonstrated that PNAd-positive HEVs form a discrete endothelial cluster characterized by high expression of adhesion genes such as  SELE ,  SELP ,  B3GNT3  and  CHST4 , whereas BECs segregate as a separate population lacking immune-trafficking functions. These observations are consistent with our findings, supporting the conclusion that TLS maturation is conserved across different organs and tumor types.  ID1 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcriptional regulator lacking a DNA-binding motif. Instead, it heterodimerizes with canonical bHLH factors, blocking lineage-specific transcription and sustaining a proliferative, undifferentiated state. Its expression is induced by a variety of upstream cues, including BMP/SMAD1-5, TGF-β, VEGF-A/VEGFR2, hypoxia-stabilized HIF-1α, Wnt/β-catenin, and inflammatory cytokines [ 41 ]. In tumors,  ID1  is enriched mainly in malignant and endothelial cells and promotes metastasis and angiogenesis; therefore, its overexpression correlates with poor prognosis. However, its involvement in HEVs remains unreported [ 42 ]. Lyden et al. showed that physiological  ID  expression is indispensable for angiogenesis in  ID  knockout mouse models, in which endothelial cells lacking  ID1  emerged in tumor xenografts but did not lumenize or generate properly branched vessels [ 43 ]. Accordingly, ID family genes are critical for synchronizing endothelial differentiation with the invasive expansion of the vascular network. Typically, high  ID1  expression in bulk lung tumor tissue is linked to poor prognosis, whereas our data show that within TLSs, elevated  ID1  levels trend toward improved clinical outcomes [ 44 ]. Such  ID1 -like “context-dependent inversions” are likewise observed for several other genes within the TLS compartment. Although the  CXCL12–CXCR4  axis is classically pro-tumorigenic outside TLSs, promoting metastasis, angiogenesis, and immune evasion through ERK1/2, Ras, p38 MAPK, PLC/MAPK, and JNK cascades [ 45 ], CXCL12 expression in combined hepatocellular–cholangiocarcinoma correlates positively with TLS density, TLS maturation, and favorable prognosis, suggesting that within TLSs this axis may instead support lymphoid organization and maturation [ 38 ]. In parallel, a recent study in hepatocellular carcinoma demonstrated that chemotherapy-induced TLS formation is likewise driven by CXCL12–CXCR4–mediated recruitment of immune and stromal cells, further reinforcing the notion that this axis can acquire a TLS-promoting role in specific therapeutic contexts [ 46 ]. Collectively, these observations highlight that signaling pathways traditionally viewed as oncogenic can adopt distinct, TLS-restricted functions, underscoring the need to dissect TLS-specific vascular pathways when developing HEV-focused immuno-oncology strategies.  CXCL13 is a recognized marker of follicular TLS cores and favorable outcome [ 14 ,  47 ]. In our data, the CXCL13 load per TLS was comparable between the control and ICB-treated cohorts, whereas CXCR5 expression was increased in ICB-treated TLSs. This dissociation suggests that ICB does not globally amplify CXCL13 production itself, but rather selectively enhances the responsiveness of B cells and Tfh to a relatively stable CXCL13 field. By contrast, knowledge regarding chemokines other than CXCL13 remains limited. Our data show that ICB selectively augments  CXCL12  expression in fibroblasts. Although the mechanistic link between PD-1 signaling and  CXCL12  induction remains to be elucidated, the increase in CXCL12 parallels a modest association between PD-L1 TPS and TLS maturation [ 13 ]. Consistent with independent spatial omics studies, mature TLSs displayed strikingly high  CXCL12  levels, mirroring the  CXCL13  pattern, suggesting that, in this compartmentalized niche,  CXCL12  may emerge as a biomarker of durable benefits in immunotherapy-treated patients rather than a canonical pro-tumorigenic signal [ 38 ]. Nevertheless, multivariate models incorporating TLS maturation as a confounder did not identify CXCL12 as an independent predictor, underscoring the need for cautious interpretation. In contrast, ID1 retained its independent prognostic significance even after adjustment, despite possible unmeasured immunosuppressive factors limiting its predictive value. Although our study is retrospective and does not allow longitudinal tracking of individual HEVs, one possible interpretation is that an ID1-high, functionally active HEV niche is well established at baseline in tumors that ultimately respond to ICB. In contrast, such an ID1-high niche may be insufficiently formed or inadequately maintained in non-responders. These post-treatment changes do not contradict the prognostic relevance of baseline ID1-high HEVs. Baseline ID1-high HEVs in untreated tumors reflect a reactive, lymphocyte-recruiting program that facilitates antitumor immunity and predicts ICI benefit, similar to reports showing that pre-existing HEV-rich tumors are associated with improved clinical outcomes [ 48 ]. In contrast, the ID1-low, PNAd-low, angiogenic-signature–high state observed after ICI likely represents a physiological reprogramming process during the resolution of inflammation, in which HEVs transition from a recruitment-competent phenotype to a vascular-maintenance or retention-type state. Thus, the baseline predictive role of ID1 and its post-therapy reduction correspond to distinct temporal phases of HEV biology rather than opposing biological effects. In summary, our work illustrates ID1 as a novel predictive and monitoring biomarker, although its regulatory mechanisms require further research.  The principal strength of this study was the application of Xenium In Situ, which preserved the native continuity of TLSs and their vasculature while providing single-cell resolution. Conventional scRNA-seq–derived “TLS-mimic” datasets cannot attain this fidelity: our approach profiled > 300,000 TLS-resident cells and retained intact follicles and vessels, which allowed the direct assessment of CCIs and HEV-mediated lymphocyte recruitment. We then validated the markers identified through this spatial screening in independent immunotherapy cohorts, thereby establishing ID1 as a clinically relevant biomarker associated with survival. However, the study has several limitations. First, the target-gene panel was relatively small. Although the default set captures core cell-type markers, it does not include essential TLS genes such as  BCL6  and  AICDA , which should be custom-added for deeper analyses. Second, the discovery and validation cohorts were modest in size and retrospective in design; thus, selection bias was possible, and the generalizability of the findings is limited. To address these issues, a prospective study with a larger patient cohort is warranted.  In conclusion, our data revealed a link between TLS maturation or ICB therapy and HEC differentiation, in which  ID1  plays a pivotal regulatory role. In mature TLSs, HECs display high  ID1  expression, actively recruit lymphocytes, and are associated with favorable clinical outcomes. However, after ICB induced tumor regressions,  ID1  and adhesion transcripts in HECs decreased sharply, lymphocyte ingress wanes, and a vascular remodeling-signature was induced. Therefore, ID1 has emerged as a dynamic biomarker in patients treated with immunotherapy. Collectively, these findings provide a mechanistic framework and a practical biomarker set for HEV-focused immuno-oncology strategies.    Supplementary Information

evidence_text:
Single-Cell Lineage Trajectory Defines Cyclin-Dependent Kinase Inhibitor-Sensitive Cells-of-Origin in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

Background and aims

Understanding the cells of origin is essential for overcoming therapy resistance and improving early intervention strategies in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Despite recent advances in genomic profiling, the precise cellular hierarchies and molecular programs driving ESCC initiation remain poorly defined.

Methods

We utilized machine learning-based single-cell trajectory analysis on 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide-induced murine models and genetically engineered organoids to identify cellular lineages during tumorigenesis. Combined with gene regulatory network analysis, we identified transcriptional drivers of tumor initiation and employed transcriptome-based drug repurposing to predict compounds targeting these initiating populations.

Results

Our analyses revealed multiple distinct epithelial clusters that function as cellular origins of ESCC, exhibiting diverse stem and progenitor signatures. Gene regulatory network analysis of these populations indicated activation of stem/progenitor cell regulators, including CEBPβ and TFAP2A/C. Translating these findings, a transcriptome-based drug repurposing screen identified 5 chemical candidates, 4 of which are potent cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, aligning with the frequent loss-of-function mutations in TP53 and CDKN2A observed in ESCC. Notably, CDK inhibitors markedly inhibit ESCC cell proliferation.

Conclusion

This research delineates the potential cellular origins of ESCC and their key regulons, thereby pioneering a single-cell-derived therapeutic strategy that exposes vulnerabilities in tumor-initiating cells.

evidence_text:
High-definition spatial transcriptomic profiling of immune cell populations in colorectal cancer. A comprehensive understanding of cellular behavior and response to the tumor microenvironment (TME) in colorectal cancer (CRC) remains elusive. Here, we introduce the high-definition Visium spatial transcriptomic technology (Visium HD) and investigate formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded human CRC samples (n = 5). We demonstrate the high sensitivity, single-cell-scale resolution and spatial accuracy of Visium HD, generating a highly refined whole-transcriptome spatial profile of CRC samples. We identify transcriptomically distinct macrophage subpopulations in different spatial niches with potential pro-tumor and anti-tumor functions via interactions with tumor and T cells. In situ gene expression analysis validates our findings and localizes a clonally expanded T cell population close to macrophages with anti-tumor features. Our study demonstrates the power of high-resolution spatial technologies to understand cellular interactions in the TME and paves the way for larger studies that will unravel mechanisms and biomarkers of CRC biology, improving diagnosis and disease management strategies. Main  CRC accounted for 9.4% of cancer-related deaths (0.9 million) in 2020, and its global incidence is predicted to double by 2035 (refs.   1 , 2  ). Its poor 5-year survival rate highlights the need for better early detection and prognostic biomarkers for future disease management  3  . Growing evidence suggests that tumor heterogeneity is best described at the transcriptome level, rather than with classical histopathological or mutation-centered disease classifications  4  . Technologies that refine our understanding of the TME, including the diverse roles of innate and adaptive immune responses and cellular crosstalk in CRC, have the potential to inform better clinical intervention strategies.  Sequencing-based genomic technologies have played an important role in building our knowledge of CRC biology  4 – 7  . However, bulk sequencing, which involves averages data from cells and tissues, is confounded by the complexities of the TME and intratumor heterogeneity. Single-cell transcriptomic (single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq)) technologies have partially filled this gap and allowed for detailed exploration of the cell types within the TME in CRC  8 – 16  . Although these studies add critical single-cell-level resolution to our understanding of CRC, they lack any information about the cellular organization within the tissue. Spatial transcriptomics offers a solution. Several commercial technologies are currently available, including Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression (‘Visium v2’, 10x Genomics), STOmics (BGI) and Curio Seeker (Curio Bioscience). Other published methods include Seq-Scope  17  , Nova-ST  18  , Open-ST  19  , HDST  20  , DBiT-seq  21  , Pixel-seq  22   and XYZeq  23  . These methods have enabled the localization of cell types within tissues, which is critical for understanding the interaction between cells in the TME of CRC  24 – 27  . However, these technologies lack resolution at the single-cell scale or are typically only compatible with freshly frozen tissues, and, as such, a deep understanding of tumor organization based on readily available biobanked samples remains elusive.  Here, we introduce Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (‘Visium HD’), a whole-transcriptome assay with single-cell-scale resolution compatible with freshly frozen, fixed frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples. The Visium HD slides provide a dramatically increased oligonucleotide barcode density (~11,000,000 continuous 2-µm features in a 6.5 × 6.5-mm Visium HD capture area, compared to ~5,000 55-µm features with gaps between the equivalent Visium v2 capture area), generating data that can be binned in square features. We demonstrate the use of Visium HD as a discovery platform by profiling CRC FFPE tissue blocks from multiple patients. The single-cell-scale resolution of Visium HD allowed us to map distinct populations of immune cells, specifically macrophages and T cells, and evaluate DGE at the tumor boundary. We also generated a multi-patient single-cell reference dataset from a larger cohort of FFPE samples and used it to annotate deconvolved Visium HD data bins, validating the cell type populations identified by Visium HD and subsequently using the integrated data to comprehensively map the cellular composition and molecular signatures of the TME in CRC. Leveraging the high resolution of Visium HD, we examined the cells at the immediate periphery (within 50 µm) of the tumor. This allowed us to spatially map distinct macrophage subpopulations to specific tumor regions, to compare their transcriptomic profiles, which indicate that they may exert pro-tumor roles via different pathways, and to characterize cell–cell interactions. To validate the spatial accuracy of Visium HD, we analyzed a subset of genes using an independent spatial technology (Xenium In Situ Gene Expression  28  ). We confirmed the presence of the two pro-tumor macrophage subpopulations in different tumor niches and pinpointed the location of the T cells within the TME. We also detected a clonally expanded T cell population and the microenvironment in which it resides, revealing a macrophage-containing niche with anti-tumor features.  Our study underscores the importance of using high-resolution spatial technologies in exploring the heterogeneity of cancer biology. These advanced tools are crucial for precisely mapping diverse immune cell niches and elucidating the complex interactions between these cells and their microenvironment. Spatial technologies provide a detailed understanding of spatial variations in cell types, their subpopulations and cell-to-cell relationships, which are key to developing targeted therapies and personalized treatment approaches. The combination of whole-transcriptome and targeted in situ spatial technologies used in our investigation provides a deep insight into the complex and dynamic nature of the TME, highlighting the importance of spatial context in understanding cancer heterogeneity and disease progression.    Results  Visium HD enables transcriptome-wide spatial gene expression analysis at single-cell scale. Gene expression is measured by the capture of ligated probe pairs targeting the whole protein-coding transcriptome. We profiled tumor biopsies from five patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma, in addition to normal adjacent tissue (NAT) from three of these patients (Table  1 ). Serial sections of FFPE tissues were used to benchmark the technology performance or to explore the TME using Visium HD. Additionally, selected serial sections were used to generate an scRNA-seq dataset and for in situ gene expression analysis (Fig.  1 ). Visium HD specifications and performance  The Visium HD capture array consists of 2 × 2-µm squares of uniquely barcoded oligonucleotides directly adjacent to each other on the slide, resulting in a continuous lawn of capture oligonucleotides. This represents an increase of several orders of magnitude in barcode complexity over earlier Visium slides, which have 55-µm circular capture areas with a 100-µm center to center gaps between them (Fig.  2a,b ). For downstream analysis, the Space Ranger (version 3.0) pipeline outputs the raw 2-µm data and data binned at 8- and 16-µm resolution. Unless otherwise described, we used the 8-µm binned data in our analyses. Source data                    To assess Visium HD performance, we analyzed serial sections from a normal colon mucosa sample run on Visium v2 and Visium HD. Visium HD generated notably higher-resolution data, as shown by the improved unsupervised clustering, both in terms of the refined specificity of the clusters and the ability to map them to morphological features of the colon mucosal tissue (Fig.  2c ). Whole-transcriptome unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts at similar sequencing depth showed a strong correlation between the two technologies (Fig.  2d ,  R  2  = 0.82 and Extended Data Fig.  1 ,  R  2  = 0.81 and 0.90), indicating that the Visium HD assay maintains the high assay sensitivity of Visium v2 (Supplementary Table  1 ).  Source data 
                   The estimated fraction of molecules arising from off-target probe binding events, that is, probes binding to genomic DNA (gDNA), was reduced in Visium HD (average of 4.13% in Visium v2 and 0.70% in Visium HD) (Supplementary Table  1 ). To assess any potential bias arising from such events, these probes were computationally excluded for this analysis, after which we observed a stronger correlation between the UMI counts from the different assays ( R  2  = 0.92, Fig.  2d ;  R  2  = 0.93 and 0.96, Extended Data Fig.  1 ).  In array-based spatial technologies, the analyte to be measured (messenger RNA (mRNA) itself or a ligated probe reporting on the mRNA) must move from the tissue to come in contact with the array. Precise transfer of analytes with minimal lateral movement is essential to ensure that the spatial transcript measurements are representative of the biology of the tissue being analyzed. To achieve this, tissue placement and subsequent molecular biology reactions must be carefully controlled to minimize lateral movement of transcripts or their proxies away from the site of origin. Similar to the Visium v2 assay, Visium HD uses the CytAssist instrument. The CytAssist controls reagent flow and thus allows target molecules from the tissue to be captured upon release, preventing free diffusion of transcripts and ensuring accurate transfer of analytes from tissues to the capture arrays. The spatial fidelity gains afforded by the CytAssist have been described previously  29 , 30   (technical note  CG000618 , revision B). To quantify the spatial accuracy of Visium HD, we analyzed genes with distinct localization to the glands of normal colon mucosal tissue (goblet cell gene markers:  CLCA1 ,  FCGBP  and  MUC2 ). In each tissue section, we manually selected four regions of interest (ROIs) and, for each marker gene, quantified the number of UMIs that were within or outside of the annotated structures in which their expression is expected based on established expression patterns  31  . Visium HD maps the landscape of CRC at single-cell scale  We profiled three CRC samples using Visium HD and combined them into a single dataset. An initial analysis of the combined dataset identified 23 clusters grouped into nine major cell types (tumor, intestinal epithelial, endothelial, smooth muscle, T cells, fibroblasts, B cells, myeloid, neuronal) and one unknown cluster (a cell cluster with a gene expression profile that did not readily match any known cell type), which aligned with the expected morphological features of the tissues (Fig.  3a ). As an orthogonal measurement of cells present in normal and diseased colon samples, we generated a single-cell reference atlas of 260,506 cells from serial FFPE sections of normal and CRC tissues ( n  = 8; Table  1 ). Differential gene expression (DGE) analysis of the cells in this atlas allowed us to annotate cell types based on published cell gene markers (Extended Data Fig.  3 ). We used this dataset as a reference to deconvolve the HD data, which yielded a highly resolved map of the cell types within the tissue resembling the expected tissue morphology (Fig.  3b ). Each patient sample was associated with a major and distinct tumor cell type (Extended Data Figs.  4  and  5 ) that mapped onto the tumor regions across each tissue section. We validated the spatial arrangement of these cell labels in Visium HD with the expression of well-known markers such as  PIGR  (goblet cells and enterocytes) , CEACAM6  (tumor) and  COL1A1  (fibroblasts) (Fig.  3c ). When we compared the unsupervised clustering to the deconvolution results, we found that cell types with stereotypical morphological organization (for example, goblet cells and enterocytes in colon glands) can be identified based on the Visium HD clustering data alone. However, deconvolution based on single-cell data was useful for identifying subtypes of cells with a more random organization or very small cells, for example, B cell and T cell subtypes (Extended Data Fig.  6 ).                      Tumor boundary analysis reveals macrophage subpopulations  As immune cell dynamics are known to play a key role in CRC progression, we used the Visium HD data to characterize the immune cell populations proximal to tumor cells. We used a custom distance-based analysis to identify all barcoded 8-µm bins within 50 µm of the regions we had labeled as tumor cells via spot deconvolution (Fig.  4a ). We reasoned that a 50-µm radius around tumor cells was likely to contain cells that are either directly interacting with the tumor cells or influencing the TME. We quantified the cellular composition of these regions compared to those identified in the rest of the tissue. In all tissue blocks, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) were the most prominent cell type while macrophages were consistently identified as the most abundant immune cell type (Fig.  4b ) in regions proximal to tumor cells. We corroborated these findings by examining the expression of known macrophage ( C1QC ) and CAF ( COL1A1 ) markers (Fig.  4a ). T cells exhibit clonally expanded niches within the CRC TME  It is known that T cell-infiltrated tumors have more positive patient outcomes than those with T cells excluded  34   and that the functional state of these infiltrated cells is also important  35  . Thus, we explored the localization and function of T cells in our samples. Our periphery analysis identified T cells, but using the 8 × 8-μm binned data meant that most T cells in the tumor periphery were assigned to doublet bins or rejected (the algorithm was unable to predict the cell type) and therefore excluded, making them challenging to localize (Fig.  6a  and Extended Data Fig.  8 ). To mitigate this, we leveraged the 2 × 2-µm data and assigned bins that were located within segmented nuclear polygons to create a gene-by-nucleus UMI count matrix for further processing (Fig.  6b ). Using this approach, we identified T cells at the tumor boundary (Fig.  6c ). We also examined the expression of known T cell markers ( TRAC  and  CD3E ) and other cell type markers, including  PECAM1  (endothelial),  IGKC  (plasma),  COL1A1  (CAF),  SPP1  or  SELENOP  (macrophages) and  CEACAM5  (tumor) (Extended Data Fig.  9 ) to obtain a fine-grained map of the cell types in these tissue areas. Through this analysis, we identified and localized both CD4 +  and CD8 +  T cells at the tumor periphery but not in the surrounding normal tissue, suggesting that these infiltrating lymphocytes may be playing an active anti-tumor role.
